A shiver is a sudden, brief, involuntary trembling or shaking of your body — or a part of it. "Involuntary" here is key: it means your body does it on its own, without you deciding to. You don't choose to shiver; it just happens to you.

Think of it as a tiny wave of shaking that moves through your body in an instant and then stops.

A shiver doesn't happen randomly — there's always a trigger. The most common triggers are:

1. Cold
When you step outside in freezing weather, your body might produce a shiver (or many of them) to generate warmth. This is the most everyday, familiar use of the word.

2. Fear, horror, or dread
When something frightens or disgusts you deeply, you can feel a shiver. This kind of shiver often moves specifically along your spine or the back of your neck.

A shiver ran down his spine as he heard the strange sound in the dark hallway.

3. Excitement or anticipation
Good feelings can also cause a shiver — the kind you feel just before something thrilling or wonderful is about to happen.

She felt a shiver of excitement as the curtain began to rise.

4. Illness or fever
When your body is fighting a sickness, shivers are common. The body shakes as part of its temperature regulation process.

This distinction is important.

  • A shiver (singular) = one single, brief trembling moment.
  • The shivers (plural) = a repeated, ongoing state of shivering, usually caused by illness or extreme cold.

"I've got the shivers — I think I'm coming down with a fever."

When you say someone "has the shivers," it means they are shaking repeatedly, not just once.

"A shiver ran down my spine"
This is one of the most common expressions in English. It means you suddenly felt a strong emotion — usually fear, dread, or sometimes awe — so intensely that it produced a physical shiver along your back.

"A shiver of [emotion]"
Here, "shiver" is used figuratively to mean a sudden, fleeting feeling of some emotion — fear, excitement, pleasure, disgust, etc.

A shiver of disgust passed through her as she read the letter.
He felt a shiver of delight at the news.

Notice how in these cases, "shiver" describes the emotion itself as something brief, quick, and intense — just like the physical shaking it refers to.

"Give someone the shivers"
If something "gives you the shivers," it makes you feel uneasy, afraid, or deeply uncomfortable — sometimes literally cold, sometimes just psychologically unsettling.

That old abandoned house gives me the shivers.
A Less Common Meaning: Small Fragments

There is a secondary meaning of "shiver" as a noun, though you'll see it far less frequently. It can refer to a small, thin splinter or fragment — usually of glass, wood, or stone — left behind when something hard shatters.

The vase hit the floor and broke into shivers of glass.

This meaning connects to the same idea of something breaking apart quickly and sharply, just as a shiver of the body is a sudden, sharp little movement.

A shiver is about something sudden, brief, and beyond your control — whether it's the physical trembling of your body in the cold or in fear, a momentary flash of emotion, or a tiny sharp fragment of something broken. The word always carries this quality of quickness and involuntariness. Something shivers; something produces shivers — but it always happens in an instant, almost before you notice it.
